newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH FOREST EMPLOYERS MUM ON PAPER UNION VIEWS.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH FOREST EMPLOYERS MUM ON PAPER UNION VIEWS.

text.p: The Finnish Forest Industries Federation said on Monday it would make no comment on the views about the coming pay deal in the paper industry voiced over the weekend by paper workers' union chairman Jarmo Lahteenmaki.
"We have no comment. We have read about in in the papers and we have no comment," a senior official at the federation told Reuters by telephone.
Mauri Moren, deputy managing director of the federation and its chief incomes settlement negotiator, was on vacation and not available for comment, his secretary said.

In the text of a speech prepared for delivery at a union meeting on Saturday, Lahteenmaki said export companies needed their own funding and reserves arrangements to ensure smooth payout of salaries to workers regardless of business cycle fluctuations.

"Unless a balancing system is created in Finland, the only possibility for workers in cyclically sensitive sectors to take precautions for the worse years to come is to sharply raise wages in good economic times," Lahteenmaki said.
"The experience of the last decades in the paper industry is that, without balancing arrangements, money left with the company in good years is money left with its owners," he said.
"It does not save the workers from being treated badly when demand weakens," he added.
A situation like this lay in store for the coming pay talks on a new deal scheduled to start early in 1998, Lahteenmaki said.

"We must first consider what is the workers' fair share of the results of the production. This estimate will be influenced by dividend payouts, which look quite abundant, by options schemes for executives and by the strong rise in raw wood prices," he said.

"The second matter under consideration is whether we can act with long-term interests in mind or whether the only practical possibility is to go for as quick and direct an increase in earnings as possible," he said.

Looking at the coming autumn's incomes settlement negotiations, Lahteenmaki said the paper workers' union found it necessary to reserve for itself the option to go for branch-level collective bargaining talks.
He repeated the union's concern that the Finnish paper industry might face significant losses if Finland joined European economic and monetary union and the dollar suddenly weakened.
"If the North American economy runs into trouble the dollar will weaken and forest industry products which are cheap in euros will flood Europe," Lahteenmaki said.
"Finland can lose tens of billions as production and prices collapse," he said, noting that the North American competitors' production costs were in dollars.

Under the threat of such a scenario the forest industry was transferring production to Central Europe and even to other continents. Another tactic used by employers was to rely ever more on temporary workers, he said.

The paper workers' union wanted to develop production and quality with the help of permanently employed staff, Lahteenmaki said, adding that wages were a small cost factor in the capital intensive forest and paper industry.
